summary: The build can start: the machine has Node.js/npx, the DocumentDB MCP server, the DocumentDB skill pack, and Microsoft Learn search available. Key facts about the service were verified and corrected (resource type, CLI commands, connection string shape, local gateway port, vector / full-text APIs). Gaps that slow the build but have workarounds: mongosh is not installed (helps manual verification), some older CosmosDB-flavored commands or examples appear in the cold answers and must not be used, and a local DocumentDB gateway container is not running (Docker present).
summary_points: All required agent skills (documentdb-*) and the documentdb MCP server are installed and available, so code + verification against the live cluster can proceed.

Several cold answers were incorrect or outdated (resource type, az CLI command group, connection-string host/port, index creation for search/vector); use the DocumentDB skills and Learn pages to correct them before coding.
Node/npx and npm tooling are available for building the Node.js LangChain sample; Docker is present so the team can run a local gateway if desired, but no local gateway container is running.
mongosh is not on PATH — useful for manual checks but not strictly required because the documentdb MCP server exposes read/write and index tools.
Verdict = ready_with_gaps: build can start, but the builder must follow the corrected facts and either install mongosh or rely on the MCP server and Learn docs for verification.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for a cluster/account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (for Cosmos DB / DocumentDB accounts).
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider: Microsoft.DocumentDB. The cluster resource type for this managed Mongo offering is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (API versions such as 2025-09-01).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared namespace Microsoft.DocumentDB and legacy usage of 'databaseAccounts' for Cosmos DB led the cold answer to return the older Cosmos DB account resource type instead of the newer mongoClusters resource for the dedicated vCore-style DocumentDB offering.
confusions.build_risk: Using Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in IaC or az CLI calls would target the Cosmos DB account API, not the mongoClusters resource; deployments would fail or produce the wrong resource type.
improvements: Update the 'Quickstart' and 'deploy' docs and README samples to explicitly show Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for DocumentDB clusters (example: quickstart-bicep and CLI examples).
Add a short note in the agent kit 'deploy' guidance: 'Use resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts) for vCore DocumentDB clusters.'

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in Azure CLI group az cosmosdb (core CLI). Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRG --kind MongoDB ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb command group (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster show). The DocumentDB command group provides mongocluster subcommands; these are in the CLI command surface (preview commands under az documentdb).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB 'az cosmosdb' command group manages Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (Cosmos DB). The service rename and new mongoClusters resource make 'az documentdb' the right group; older examples (and Cosmos DB docs) caused the mix-up.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb create (older Cosmos DB docs)

confusions.build_risk: Following the az cosmosdb example could create different kinds of Cosmos resources or fail to create the new managed Mongo 'mongoClusters' resource; automation would target incorrect APIs.
improvements: Change the sample prompt and agent-kit quickstarts to call out 'az documentdb mongocluster create' explicitly and deprecate references to 'az cosmosdb' for this offering.
Add a short CLI migration note in the 'Deploy' skill: 'If you used az cosmosdb for the older Cosmos account workflows, use az documentdb mongocluster for vCore clusters.'

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource of type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts'. Terraform (azurerm provider): resource 'azurerm_cosmosdb_account'.
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM: use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type (API examples and templates reference this). Terraform (AzureRM): prefer azurerm_mongo_cluster (or the AzAPI mapping to Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters); older azurerm_cosmosdb_account targets Cosmos DB databaseAccounts and is not the correct resource for a dedicated DocumentDB cluster.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Terraform/Bicep examples for Cosmos DB used databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account. The new vCore DocumentDB cluster uses a distinct resource type (mongoClusters) and the Terraform provider exposes a dedicated azurerm_mongo_cluster resource or AzAPI mapping.
confusions.build_risk: Authoring Bicep/Terraform that provision databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account would not create the vCore mongoCluster; IaC would be wrong and may produce resources with different capabilities/charge model.
improvements: Update the 'examples/azure-deployment' templates and the skill README to show Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and the Terraform azurerm_mongo_cluster example.
Add a short one-line note in the agent kit: 'Do not use azurerm_cosmosdb_account for vCore DocumentDB clusters; use azurerm_mongo_cluster / mongoClusters resource.'

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters use mongodb+srv (recommended) or mongodb URIs with host suffix <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (or <cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com for single-cluster). TLS is required (tls=true), retryWrites must be false, and authMechanism is typically SCRAM-SHA-256 for native users or MONGODB-OIDC for Microsoft Entra ID flows; the legacy port 10255 and host patterns like <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com are from older Cosmos DB styles and are not the canonical endpoints for mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB for Mongo API / legacy Cosmos account endpoints used a different host suffix and port (e.g., *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255). Similar names and overlap in 'DocumentDB' wording led the cold answer to return the older host/port pattern.

confusion_sources.title: Examples and legacy Cosmos DB connection docs (databaseAccounts)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix or port will cause connection failures or TLS/auth errors; using replicaSet=globaldb is an older Cosmos option and may be invalid for the new cluster endpoints.
improvements: Update sample READMEs and agent-kit examples to show the mongodb+srv pattern with the *.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com host and to explicitly set retryWrites=false and tls=true.
Add a short connector checklist in the driver-sample README: 'Use the portal's Connection strings panel and verify the host ends with mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com; do not assume port 10255.'

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is typically billed as a managed compute tier (vCore-style machine sizes for Mongo clusters; examples use M-series tiers such as M30) plus storage and I/O; not per-request-unit (RU) like Cosmos SQL.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters are provisioned and billed by compute tier (M10, M20, M30, etc.) and storage; this is different from the RU-based Cosmos DB (NoSQL) billing model.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (pricing and compute model)

confusions.build_risk: None — builder should pick Mxx tier per skill_md.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary auth is MongoDB username/password (SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-256). The service also supports Microsoft Entra ID: obtain an AAD access token and provide it to the driver as the credential (driver configured with authMechanism and the token as the password).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native SCRAM-SHA-256 credentials and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) flows. Entra-based auth is commonly used with the authMechanism MONGODB-OIDC and connection strings that use a client-id / OIDC mechanism; interactive or token-exchange flows are driven by OIDC configuration rather than simply passing an AAD access token as the Mongo 'password' in every driver – follow the Learn 'role-based access control' guidance and the DocumentDB connection guidance for the exact patterns.
confusions.grounding_source: Learn 'Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control' and documentdb-mcp-setup

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control (Learn)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer conflated generic 'AAD token-as-password' patterns with the specific MONGODB-OIDC integration and missed the recommended authMechanism and connection-string forms for Entra; older blogs describing naive token-passing caused the mix-up.
confusions.build_risk: Implementing Entra auth by simply requesting an AAD token and using it as the Mongo 'password' with an unrelated authMechanism can fail to authenticate; the app may be unable to connect with Entra identities.
improvements: In the agent kit's connection guidance, add an explicit Entra example using authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and link to the portal's 'Connection strings -> Microsoft Entra ID' section.
Add a small snippet in the driver-sample README showing the exact connection string pattern for both native (SCRAM-SHA-256) and Entra (MONGODB-OIDC) authentication.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB client libraries for your language (e.g. official Node.js driver 'mongodb' or Mongoose). There is no special DocumentDB runtime client library for application data plane; Azure SDKs are only for management/ARM operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the official MongoDB drivers (Node.js 'mongodb', Mongoose, etc.) for data-plane operations. Azure SDKs are for control-plane/management tasks.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn quickstarts and documentdb-driver skill

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported vector index types include DiskANN, HNSW and IVF. Example: db.carts.createIndex( { embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vectorIndexType: 'HNSW', dimensions: 768, metric: 'cosine', efConstruction: 200, M: 48 } ).
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB supports vector index subtypes (vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, vector-ivf) and provides a service-specific vector creation API documented in the vector-search guidance (index creation is done via DocumentDB's vector/createSearchIndexes interfaces and 'cosmosSearch' query usage; the exact index-creation command is provider-specific and the documentdb-vector-search skill shows the recommended commands and parameter names). The raw createIndex(...) snippet above is not the canonical command to create an indexed vector in DocumentDB.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reused a MongoDB-style createIndex example; DocumentDB's vector/index creation uses provider-specific 'cosmosSearch' / createSearchIndexes semantics and different option names.
confusions.build_risk: Attempting to create a vector index with createIndex using unsupported options will fail; queries expecting vector indexes will return errors or not use the intended index.
improvements: Replace generic createIndex examples with the DocumentDB vector-index creation examples (vector-create-diskann, vector-create-hnsw) in the agent kit and sample README.
Add a short code snippet in the sample that calls the DocumentDB 'createSearchIndexes' / vector index API for the sample collection.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text/hybrid search is done by integrating the cluster with a search service (Azure Cognitive Search) or by using the service's built-in vector + text search features when available.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB exposes built-in full-text search via createSearchIndexes + the $search aggregation stage, and also supports hybrid retrieval combining BM25 and vector (cosmosSearch) on the same collection. External Cognitive Search is an option but is not required — the native createSearchIndexes / $search + cosmosSearch path is the recommended DocumentDB approach for integrated lexical + vector search.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many prior migration guides show pushing data into Azure Cognitive Search; the cold answer mixed that pattern with DocumentDB's native $search/cosmosSearch functionality.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder chooses an external Cognitive Search data pipeline instead of the native createSearchIndexes + $search approach, the sample will become more complex (ETL) and will not demonstrate DocumentDB's built-in search capabilities.
improvements: Document the recommended native $search + createSearchIndexes usage in the sample README and show a short hybrid example combining BM25 + cosmosSearch.
Mark older 'push-to-Cognitive-Search' quickstarts as 'alternate approach' and prefer native $search snippets in canonical samples.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cluster supports MongoDB server/wire protocol version 7.0 (and recent 6.x compatibility).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0; it implements a high degree of operator compatibility (99.03%) but administrative commands and a small set of operators may differ — consult the compatibility reference for details.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer understated the supported wire-protocol range (named 7.0 only); updated docs show broader support (5.0–8.0).
confusions.build_risk: Assuming only 7.0 may lead a builder to pin an unnecessary driver version or miss newer features available in 5–8 support range.
improvements: Update any sample README that pins a particular MongoDB wire protocol to document the supported range 5.0–8.0 and recommend testing with the target client driver version.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no official local emulator; run the official MongoDB Docker image (mongo:7) on port 27017 for local development.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image for local development: ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest (Gateway) which exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260; it supports TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256 and is the recommended local dev image to emulate the managed service.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed the generic MongoDB container; in reality the managed DocumentDB engine has a dedicated gateway image and uses port 10260. The shared 'Mongo wire protocol' surface hides this but the port and TLS semantics are DocumentDB-specific for the official local image.
confusions.build_risk: Testing against plain mongo:7 on 27017 will not faithfully reproduce DocumentDB features (gateway TLS, provider-specific index / search APIs, vector functionality) and will create false positives/negatives in tests.
improvements: Add a short 'Local dev' section in sample README: how to start the DocumentDB gateway container (image and port 10260) and recommended Docker run / docker-compose example.
Add a docker-compose file to the sample repo that starts the local gateway and seeds sample data.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported only when the cluster exposes a replica-set/oplog interface; some managed clusters require enabling an oplog or a specific cluster tier to get change stream support.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported in Azure DocumentDB. For multi-shard clusters, a feature (Change streams for multishard clusters) may need to be enabled in the portal; single-cluster change streams work with the standard driver APIs. Use the DocumentDB 'Change streams' docs for exact enablement steps when working with multishard clusters.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn 'Change streams in Azure DocumentDB'
confusions.build_risk: None if you follow the Learn page; remember to enable the portal feature for multishard change streams if your sample needs cluster-wide change streams.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The service is covered by the 'documentdb' MCP server (service-specific MCP server). Use the documentdb MCP server's default profile to obtain data-plane inspection and index tools. The general Azure MCP server does not provide the service-specific inspection capabilities for DocumentDB clusters.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane inspection and index management tools; the generic 'azure' MCP server is for control-plane management and best-practice lookups and does not provide the documentdb data-plane toolset.
confusions.build_risk: None — use the documentdb MCP server for cluster data-plane checks.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft used the name 'DocumentDB' for the precursor NoSQL service which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. The modern managed Mongo-compatible offering is commonly referred to as DocumentDB or Cosmos DB's Mongo API in Azure documentation; it is not the same as any unrelated open-source 'DocumentDB' project.
confusions.grounded_answer: The naming is subtle: the modern offering was previously named the vCore-based 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)'. Microsoft renamed that vCore offering to 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' to align with the open-source DocumentDB engine; it is distinct from the original Azure DocumentDB product that became Azure Cosmos DB in 2017. Azure DocumentDB (vCore) and Cosmos DB for NoSQL / RU-based Mongo API are separate services.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?
Azure DocumentDB FAQ (how it relates to Cosmos DB)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple rebrands and overlapping names over the years (original DocumentDB → Cosmos DB, vCore-based Mongo offering formerly called 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)', and the new DocumentDB name) cause name collisions in docs and blog posts.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong product name in code samples, README or IaC could mislead users and make them pick the RU-based Cosmos DB offering instead of the vCore DocumentDB cluster.
improvements: Add a short 'Naming' paragraph to the sample README: clearly say 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) — formerly

information_gaps.title: Exact sample schema fields and names
information_gaps.description: The prompt implies collections like 'customers' and 'carts' and certain fields (lastActivity/updatedAt, contactPreference, processedAt), but the skills/docs do not prescribe concrete field names and nesting shapes for the sample. The builder must choose explicit field names and document them (seed script and README). Looked in: prompt skill_md and documentdb-data-modeling, documentdb-local-deployment.

information_gaps.title: LLM provider & model selection
information_gaps.description: The prompt requests a copy-generation agent but does not specify LLM provider, model, or env var names. No installed skill states which LLM to default to. The builder must pick and document an LLM (OPENAI_API_KEY/OPENAI_MODEL or provider-agnostic abstraction). Looked in: prompt_review and available skills (none define an LLM choice).

information_gaps.title: Exact vector dimension / embedding model
information_gaps.description: The sample cluster is 'vector-capable' but the docs do not say which embedding model (dimension) the sample should use. The builder must choose an embedding model and embed-dimension (e.g., 1536) and ensure vector index 'dimensions' matches. Looked in: documentdb-vector-search and prompt skill_md.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) and manage clusters with the 'az documentdb mongocluster' CLI commands or the DocumentDB Bicep/Terraform templates that reference mongoClusters.

Use the connection string from the portal or from 'az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings' — prefer mongodb+srv with host '<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com', set tls=true and retryWrites=false, and use authMechanism SCRAM-SHA-256 for native users or MONGODB-OIDC for Entra-based authentication.

sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Create search and vector indexes using the DocumentDB-specific APIs (createSearchIndexes / cosmosSearch / vector index subtypes) instead of relying on generic createIndex BSON options; consult the documentdb-full-text-search and documentdb-vector-search skill guidance when adding indexes.

For local development, prefer the official DocumentDB gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) listening on port 10260 with TLS enabled; do not assume a vanilla mongo:7 container on 27017 reproduces DocumentDB behavior.

Use the official MongoDB Node.js driver (npm package 'mongodb') as a singleton MongoClient per process; set recommended options from the driver and set retryWrites=false for connections to DocumentDB clusters.
